title: Educational side of the workshop; Earl and George Davis
summary: Earl was drawn to teaching and playing in prisons; George Davis had a formal Juilliard background and flute, and the group sought freedom beyond formula.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Do you, did you have anything to do with like the school concept of the workshop? I know that you all had plans to maybe bring in some kids and spend some time with them. Was that more Earl's interest or yours or everybody's?

Well, I think Earl is always gravitated towards sharing the experience of trying to inform people on another level. I mean, Earl would go and play in the prisons. I mean, stuff that a lot of people would shy off from. But you've got to understand that George Davis comes from a serious educational background. And one of the greatest experiences that I've had and the things that I've learned was from my experience of playing with George. I mean, George played with the Juilliard. I mean, he is a much greater musician than most people, I guess, gives him credit for being, or even know that he is. Because George is not only a guitarist, George's major instrument was the flute. And I mean, he played as much as Hubert Laws or anybody that, as much saxophone as anybody that I know. And knows as much as much as just the whole theory and the whole formal aspect of music. I mean, these are people that have a serious background in the music. We just happen to evolve to a point where we wanted to have a freedom of expression that is beyond a particular formula. It's like being in a lab trying to discover the cure for cancer. I mean, sometimes it can come from something that is so totally obscure and from what you would normally do. And I think that's what innovation is. Trying something that is against the norm or against what people might say is the proper way to do it. You know.
